meaningful_definition.rationale: A meaningful activity is the earliest point at which a simulated user completes an action that the product is designed to reward. Views and starts show exposure or intent only; badges and level-ups are consequences awarded by the system rather than user actions.
meaningful_definition.limitations: Event-level completions cannot be tied to a preceding start within the same session (see DQ-035); 'meaningful' therefore means 'a completion was logged', not 'a full flow was observed'. Value of each action (points earned) is not in the dataset.

activation.window_rationale: Selection rule: the smallest tested window that captures the majority (≥50%) of users who activate within 60 days. Capture by window: 1d 6.2%, 3d 19.4%, 7d 35.9%, 14d 56.3%, 30d 81.0%. Short windows misclassify most eventual activators because the simulated cohort takes a median of 6.1 days to open a first session. The gain per extra day falls from 2.91pp (days 8–14) to 1.54pp (days 15–30), so 14 days is the elbow; longer windows also shrink the eligible population (902 users eligible at 14d vs 816 at 30d). The 7-day rate (45.2%) is reported alongside as an 'early activation' view.

findings.title: Most simulated users take days, not minutes, to open a first session
findings.observation: Median time from registration to first session is 6.1 days; only 13.0% of eligible users complete a meaningful activity within 1 day and 30.2% within 3 days.
findings.evidence: 14-day activation = 530/902 eligible users (58.8%); 174 users waited > 30 days for a first session.
findings.interpretation: The gap between sign-up and first use – not in-session friction – is the main activation delay in the simulated cohort.
findings.limitation: Registration timestamps carry no context (e.g. verification emails, app install) explaining the delay.
findings.product_implication: Investigate the post-registration handoff: verification flow, first-open prompts and welcome messaging.

findings.title: Once a session happens, a completed activity almost always follows
findings.observation: 984 of 984 users with a session recorded a meaningful activity; 88.4% did so within 15 minutes of their first feature event.
findings.evidence: Lifecycle: Login 984 → first meaningful 984.
findings.interpretation: In-session activation is not the bottleneck in the simulated data; getting users to the first session and back again is.
findings.limitation: Completions are 'logged', not proven end-to-end flows (completion events lack linked starts, DQ-035).
findings.product_implication: Prioritise return and first-session-delay investigations over first-session UX changes.

findings.title: Second-day return is the first major user-level drop-off
findings.observation: Among 716 users with a full 30-day horizon, 179 (25.0%) were active on only one day in their first 30 days.
findings.evidence: All-time one-day users: 158 of 984 active users; D1 return = 14.5% (142/976).
findings.interpretation: A quarter of users with sufficient observation never form a second visit.
findings.limitation: The dataset does not record why users stop or whether they received reminders.
findings.product_implication: Investigate post-first-day re-engagement (reminders, next-day reward previews).

findings.title: Progression from 3 to 7 active days is the steepest drop in the active-day ladder
findings.observation: Within the first 30 days, 102 of 392 users with 3 active days reached 7 (74.0% drop-off).
findings.evidence: Ladder (30-day horizon): 1→2 days 25.0% drop, 2→3 27.0%, 3→7 74.0%.
findings.interpretation: Short-term returners rarely become weekly habits within a month.
findings.limitation: 7 active days in 30 is an analyst threshold; the ladder is sensitive to the window.
findings.product_implication: Investigate mid-term progression mechanics (missions, levels, streaks) as habit drivers.

findings.title: Return rates depend strongly on calendar period, not on who the users are
findings.observation: D7 return rises from 26.3% for the 2026-04 first-active cohort to 56.4% for 2026-08; the daily active share of the registered base rose from 5.09% (May) to 11.34% (last 30 days).
findings.evidence: Registration-month cohorts differ (χ² p=1.2e-16); source (p=0.54) and device (p=0.87) do not.
findings.interpretation: Something time-dependent (simulation design, product changes, seasonality) drives return far more than user attributes.
findings.limitation: The dataset contains no release, campaign or notification calendar to explain the shift. TO BE VERIFIED.
findings.product_implication: Always control for cohort period when comparing groups; ask product/engineering what changed over time.

findings.title: Fast activators return more, even after controlling for join month
findings.observation: Users activating within 7 days have a 26.4pp higher fourth-week (D30) return than slower activators; within registration months the gap is 15.3pp.
findings.evidence: Logistic model of D30 return: log(hours to first activity) standardised coefficient -0.524; CV AUC 0.765 (behaviour only 0.773, calendar only 0.595).
findings.interpretation: Early activation is associated with later return; the association survives a calendar control.
findings.limitation: Association only – motivated users may both activate faster and return more (selection).
findings.product_implication: Test interventions that shorten time-to-first-activity and measure D30 return (EXP-01).

findings.title: Two in five resolved tasks end in abandonment or failure, with no dominant failure reason
findings.observation: 3,571 of 9,198 resolved task records (38.8%) were abandoned (22.3%) or failed (16.5%).
findings.evidence: Category completion rates range 59.8–62.5%; the five failure reasons each account for 701–732 records.
findings.interpretation: Task friction is broad-based rather than concentrated in one category or failure mode.
findings.limitation: failure_reason is a coarse category; no error codes, third-party responses or UI context.
findings.product_implication: Instrument detailed failure context before redesigning specific task types.

findings.title: Many task rewards sit in long-pending validation
findings.observation: 648 task records are Pending; 339 have been pending for more than 30 days at data end.
findings.evidence: Pending share by category: 5.7–7.5%.
findings.interpretation: Delayed reward confirmation may weaken the action→reward feedback loop (hypothesis).
findings.limitation: Whether users can see pending status, and validation SLAs, are not in the data. TO BE VERIFIED.
findings.product_implication: Review validation latency and pending-status visibility (EXP-04).

findings.title: Ads, CAPTCHA and Missions each lose about half of attempts
findings.observation: Watch Ads skip rate 50.3%, CAPTCHA failure rate 49.7%, Missions abandonment rate 49.9% (event level).
findings.evidence: Ads 1054 completed vs 1065 skipped; CAPTCHA 895 vs 883; Missions 702 vs 699.
findings.interpretation: These are the three features where explicit negative outcomes are logged, and all show coin-flip completion.
findings.limitation: Other features log no failure/abandon events, so their completion rates are not comparable.
findings.product_implication: Investigate ad length/reward clarity, CAPTCHA difficulty and mission scope.

findings.title: Viewing a mission or spin often does not lead to starting it
findings.observation: 375 of 901 user×feature view pairs (41.6%) for Missions and Spin the Wheel never recorded a start of the same feature.
findings.evidence: 369 pairs started without any recorded view.
findings.interpretation: Exposure does not reliably convert to engagement on these surfaces.
findings.limitation: Views and starts are not linked in-session (DQ-035); this is a user-level signal only.
findings.product_implication: Test clearer start calls-to-action on mission and spin surfaces (EXP-05).

findings.title: Sessions are short and longer sessions are not deeper
findings.observation: Median session 42s (P90 94s); duration↔events Spearman ρ = 0.027, duration↔meaningful ρ = 0.002.
findings.evidence: Short (≤P25) sessions deliver 3.35 meaningful actions/min vs 0.87 for long (>P75).
findings.interpretation: Session length is not a usable engagement proxy in the simulated data.
findings.limitation: 99.54% of completed tasks finish after their session 'ends' – session windows likely under-measure time in product.
findings.product_implication: Use completions and return frequency, not duration, as engagement KPIs; confirm session_end semantics.

findings.title: First-day sessions are the densest; later sessions are lighter
findings.observation: First-active-day sessions average 7.64 events and 2.26 meaningful actions vs 4.17 and 1.2 on later days.
findings.evidence: Mann-Whitney p = 3.3e-20; task completion is similar (61.17% vs 61.25%).
findings.interpretation: New users explore intensively on day one; returning users make shorter, more targeted visits.
findings.limitation: Day-one density may partly reflect how the simulation seeded first sessions.
findings.product_implication: Design returning-user surfaces for quick, repeatable value actions.

findings.title: Heavy first-day activity is associated with lower first-week return
findings.observation: D7 return by first-day event-volume tercile: low 55.8%, mid 52.1%, high 33.9%.
findings.evidence: In the D30 model, week-1 events have a negative standardised coefficient (-0.858) while week-1 sessions and active days are positive.
findings.interpretation: Cramming many actions into few visits looks different from spreading activity across visits.
findings.limitation: Could reflect simulation design or exhaustion of daily earning limits; not causal.
findings.product_implication: Investigate whether pacing (daily caps, 'come back tomorrow' previews) relates to return.

findings.title: Feature breadth is high and mostly mirrors activity volume
findings.observation: Active users touched a median of 13 of 15 features; 257 used all 15. Breadth vs active days Spearman ρ = 0.584.
findings.evidence: Multi-feature (≥8 features completed): 265 users (26.9% of active users).
findings.interpretation: Breadth is largely a by-product of more visits, so 'multi-feature' is not an independent engagement driver here.
findings.limitation: Simulated feature exposure may be more uniform than a real navigation structure.
findings.product_implication: Measure breadth per visit (not lifetime) when evaluating discovery changes.

findings.title: Journeys show no strong sequential structure
findings.observation: Feature-to-feature transition lifts range 0.79–1.27; session co-occurrence lifts 1.06–1.26; the most common single path covers only 1.17% of sessions.
findings.evidence: After a view, the next event is a completion about as often as after any other stage (stage-transition matrix).
findings.interpretation: Users do not follow a dominant path; no feature reliably leads to another.
findings.limitation: Event order inside sessions is unreliable (sequence numbers and timestamps disagree).
findings.product_implication: Fix event ordering instrumentation before investing in journey-based recommendations.

findings.title: Streak behaviour does not look like streaks
findings.observation: Only 23 of 533 streak claimers (4.3%) claimed on consecutive days; break events (919) ≈ claim events (922).
findings.evidence: 207 users broke a streak without any recorded claim.
findings.interpretation: Either the streak mechanic is not driving consecutive-day behaviour, or streak events are logged inconsistently.
findings.limitation: No streak length or state field exists. TO BE VERIFIED with engineering.
findings.product_implication: Add streak_started/streak_day_count events; then evaluate streak-saver ideas (EXP-06).

findings.title: Levelling up is not followed by a change in activity
findings.observation: 615 users (62.5% of active) levelled up. Around the first level-up: 1.2 active days in the prior 14 days vs 1.34 after (Wilcoxon p = 0.22, n = 187).
findings.evidence: 615 levellers recorded 1266 level-up events (2.06 per leveller).
findings.interpretation: Within the simulated data, progression milestones are not associated with a detectable activity lift.
findings.limitation: Level and XP balance are absent (level-ups counted from events); exact thresholds are simulated and documented VELOOP rules may change.
findings.product_implication: Investigate level-up feedback (reward visibility, next-goal messaging).

findings.title: Device and acquisition source show no meaningful behavioural differences
findings.observation: All Kruskal-Wallis/χ² tests across devices and sources have negligible effect sizes (max ε² = 0.004).
findings.evidence: Device activation: Android 61.08%, iOS 61.61%, Windows 49.63%, macOS 47.83% (χ² p = 0.0344, Cramér's V = 0.0979).
findings.interpretation: Observed behavioural differences are small; no device or source stands out on depth or return.
findings.limitation: Simulated acquisition sources do not represent real marketing performance; all traffic is 'Web'.
findings.product_implication: Do not prioritise device-specific fixes on this evidence; re-test with production data.

findings.title: Activity is spread evenly across hours and days of the week
findings.observation: Hour-of-day session distribution is consistent with uniform (χ² p = 0.44); weekend vs weekday trend-adjusted DAU index 1.045 vs 0.974 (p = 0.11).
findings.evidence: Weekdays hold 70.1% of events vs 71.4% of days.
findings.interpretation: The simulated data does not support time-targeted notification or maintenance-window decisions.
findings.limitation: Timestamp timezone is undocumented.
findings.product_implication: Notification-timing experiments would need production data to be meaningful.

findings.title: Pre-aggregated fields would materially change conclusions
findings.observation: events_in_session implies 10.44 events/session vs 4.689 from raw events; the milestone sheet reports 389 first logins vs 984 users with sessions.
findings.evidence: See data_quality_impact.csv for 29 before/after comparisons.
findings.interpretation: Using convenience fields without validation would mislead product decisions.
findings.limitation: Simulated data; production pipelines may differ.
findings.product_implication: Engineering: reconcile session counters, milestone generation and daily duration with raw logs.

friction.evidence: 464 users waited > 7 days for a first session; median 6.1 days.
friction.possible_explanations: Verification delays; weak welcome prompt; registration without intent; app install friction.
friction.investigation_needed: Instrument registration→verification→first-open steps; interview recent registrants.

limitations_general: Simulated users are not actual VELOOP users; no statement here describes the real platform.
No production behavioural data was used.
No reliable causal inference: all relationships are associations within synthetic data.
No guaranteed representation of the real user population (demographics, devices, sources).
Third-party activity (ad networks, task partners, validation) may not be represented accurately.
Exact production feature availability may change (VELOOP documentation notes features and mechanics can change).
Simulated timestamps are not operational logs; timezone is undocumented.
Simulated acquisition sources do not represent actual marketing performance.
Simulated retention does not represent actual VELOOP retention.
limitations_specific: No login, registration, onboarding, session or task events in the taxonomy (13 brief examples absent) – login is proxied by sessions.
Within-session event order is unreliable: sequence_number duplicates and disagrees with timestamps; completions are not linkable to starts.
Session windows (median 42 s) end before 99.54% of task completions – duration under-measures time in product.
06_Milestones contradicts raw activity and was not used as a source of truth.
04_Daily_Activity duration is inconsistent with sessions; only its event/feature counts reconcile.
current_level and xp_balance are absent: level/XP progression is limited to event counts.
platform = 'Web' for every record: platform analysis is not supported; device is used instead.
Return metrics are right-censored for recent users; windows require full observability.
Strong calendar-period effects confound any cohort comparison that does not stratify by join date.
Workbook volumes (sessions, daily records, feature usage) are below the brief's recommended ranges (source discrepancy).
Project duration differs between the workbook README (22–25 days) and the PDF (20–24 days): source discrepancy requiring confirmation.
Snapshot user attributes (account_status, onboarding_status, verification_status) have no timestamps.

reconciliation.definition_difference: ≥2 active days vs meaningful activity on ≥3 days.

reconciliation.definition_difference: Meets the breadth rule vs meets it AND every earlier funnel stage.
reconciliation.explanation: The funnel only counts multi-feature users who also returned.

reconciliation.definition_difference: ≥3 active weeks vs ≥3 active weeks AND multi-feature AND returned.
reconciliation.explanation: Cumulative counts shrink at every stage; standalone counts do not.

reconciliation.definition_difference: Any second active day, ever vs a return within days 1–7 after the first active day.

reconciliation.metrics_compared: One-time users (all time) vs one-day users in first 30 days
reconciliation.definition_difference: All active users, lifetime vs users with ≥30 observable days, first 30 days only.

reconciliation.metrics_compared: D7 return: first-active anchor vs registration anchor

catalogue.interpretation: DAU peaked at 164 (2026-09-13); DAU tracks the cumulative registered base (ρ=0.987). Spikes are statistical flags only.
catalogue.limitation: No campaign/release calendar; spikes are not attributed to causes.

catalogue.business_question: How often do users return to open sessions?
catalogue.calculation: Count of sessions per user, binned
catalogue.interpretation: 143 users have one session; median 6 sessions per active user.

catalogue.business_question: How long do sessions typically last?
catalogue.interpretation: Median 42s, P90 94s; duration is unrelated to depth (ρ=0.027).
catalogue.limitation: Session windows end before task completions (DQ-022).
catalogue.product_relevance: Do not use duration as an engagement KPI.

catalogue.business_question: What happens after a user joins?
catalogue.calculation: Cumulative user counts per stage / registered users
catalogue.interpretation: Nearly all users with a session complete an activity; the first major loss is the second active day.
catalogue.limitation: Login proxied by sessions; completions not linked to starts.
catalogue.product_relevance: Focus activation work on return and first-session delay.

catalogue.business_question: Which features reach the most users, and how many complete them?

catalogue.limitation: Exposure only known when a feature logs events.

catalogue.business_question: Which features do users come back to?
catalogue.calculation: Users with feature in ≥2 sessions / feature users
catalogue.limitation: Heavier users have more chances to repeat any feature.

catalogue.interpretation: No Recorded Activity 16; One-Time Users 158; Occasional Users 256; Returning Users 235; Multi-Feature Users 76; High-Frequency Users 259
